questions.q: What does a fire damper in a duct do?
o: Shuts automatically in a fire to keep flames from passing through a rated wall or floor
Balances airflow between duct branches during testing and commissioning
Stops outside air from blowing back in when the exhaust fan is off
Opens and closes to hold the room at its set temperature
questions.ref: ASHRAE 62.1 terminology; Grondzik and Kwok, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings
questions.n: A fire damper has a fusible link that melts and drops a curtain across the duct where it passes a fire-rated wall or floor. The others describe volume, backdraft and VAV dampers.

questions.q: Which space most commonly requires direct contaminant/moisture exhaust rather than relying only on recirculation?
o: Living room
Open office
Toilet room
Library reading area
questions.ref: ASHRAE ventilation terminology and standard HVAC design principles.
questions.n: Toilets are exhausted directly because their odor and moisture should leave the building, not be recirculated.

questions.q: Which fan type is used to move air through ductwork against high static pressure?
o: Propeller (wall) fan
Ceiling paddle fan
Centrifugal fan
Pedestal fan
questions.ref: ASHRAE 62.1 terminology; Grondzik and Kwok, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings
questions.n: A centrifugal (blower) fan throws air outward from a wheel into a scroll housing, building up pressure to push air through long ducts. Propeller fans move lots of air at very low pressure.

questions.q: What is the main role of a supply diffuser?
o: Collect room air and send it back to the air handler
Discharge stale air to the outdoors
Mix outdoor air with return air before the coil
Deliver conditioned air into a room and spread it evenly
questions.ref: ASHRAE 62.1 terminology; Grondzik and Kwok, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings
questions.n: A diffuser sits at the end of a supply duct and throws air across the room. Return grilles collect air, and exhaust louvers discharge it.

questions.q: What mainly drives stack-effect ventilation?
o: Warm indoor air being lighter than cooler outdoor air over a height
Wind pressure on the windward face of the building
Pressure from a mechanical supply fan
Moisture given off by the occupants
questions.ref: ASHRAE 62.1 terminology; Grondzik and Kwok, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings
questions.n: Warm air rises and leaves through high openings, drawing cooler air in through low ones. The taller the gap between openings and the bigger the temperature difference, the stronger the flow.

questions.q: Which term refers to air brought from outside the building for ventilation?
o: Return air
Relief air
Recirculated air
Outdoor air
questions.ref: ASHRAE ventilation terminology and standard HVAC design principles.
questions.n: Outdoor air is brought in to dilute contaminants and CO₂ produced indoors.

questions.q: In a cross-ventilated plan, what happens when full-height partitions block the path between the windward and leeward windows?
o: Airflow rises, since air speeds up around the partitions
Nothing changes, since only the window area matters
Airflow drops sharply, since air cannot pass from inlet to outlet
The room switches to stack ventilation on its own
questions.ref: ASHRAE 62.1 terminology; Grondzik and Kwok, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings
questions.n: Cross ventilation needs a clear path from the high-pressure side to the low-pressure side. Closed doors or solid partitions cut it off, whatever the window size.

questions.q: What is make-up air?
o: Air taken from a room and sent back to the air handler
Air moved between rooms through a transfer grille
Outdoor air leaking in through cracks in the envelope
Air supplied to replace air removed by exhaust systems
questions.ref: ASHRAE 62.1 terminology; Grondzik and Kwok, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings
questions.n: Kitchen hoods and large exhaust fans pull out a lot of air. Make-up air replaces it so doors do not slam and the hood keeps working.

questions.q: A 60 m³ room receives 360 m³/h of outdoor air. What is the air-change rate?
o: 6 ACH
12 ACH
3 ACH
21 ACH
questions.ref: ASHRAE 62.1 terminology; Grondzik and Kwok, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings
questions.n: Air changes per hour is the hourly airflow divided by the room volume.

questions.q: What is a return-air grille used for?
o: Delivering conditioned air into the room
Collecting room air and sending it back to the air handler
Taking in outdoor air at the building face
Discharging kitchen exhaust to the outside
questions.ref: ASHRAE 62.1 terminology; Grondzik and Kwok, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings
questions.n: Return grilles let room air leave the space and flow back to the air handler, where part of it is recirculated and part relieved.

questions.q: Which system uses fans both to supply and to exhaust air, in about equal amounts?
o: Exhaust-only ventilation
Supply-only ventilation
Balanced ventilation
Infiltration
questions.ref: ASHRAE 62.1 terminology; Grondzik and Kwok, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings
questions.n: Balanced systems control both air streams, often through a heat- or energy-recovery unit. Exhaust-only systems depressurize the space, and supply-only systems pressurize it.

questions.q: Which air stream is taken from a room and sent back toward the air handler?
o: Exhaust air
Outdoor air
Make-up air
Return air
questions.ref: ASHRAE 62.1 terminology; Grondzik and Kwok, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings
questions.n: Return air comes back to the air handler to be mixed, filtered and conditioned again. Exhaust air is thrown out of the building.

questions.q: What is infiltration?
o: Outdoor air leaking in through cracks and gaps in the envelope
Outdoor air brought in on purpose by a supply fan
Air passed from room to room through a transfer grille
Air removed from a kitchen by a range hood
questions.ref: ASHRAE 62.1 terminology; Grondzik and Kwok, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings
questions.n: Infiltration is uncontrolled. It adds cooling load and humidity, so air-conditioned buildings are sealed and given controlled outdoor air instead.

questions.q: Which approach reduces ventilation fan energy when full airflow is not always needed?
o: Running every fan at full speed around the clock
Demand-based control with variable-speed fans
Closing all outdoor-air intakes to save energy
Oversizing the fans so they run less often
questions.ref: ASHRAE 62.1 terminology; Grondzik and Kwok, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings
questions.n: CO₂ or occupancy sensors can lower airflow when fewer people are present. Fan power falls roughly with the cube of speed, so small cuts save a lot.

questions.q: A 120 m³ room needs 5 air changes per hour. What airflow is required?
o: 24 m³/h
600 m³/h
125 m³/h
questions.ref: ASHRAE 62.1 terminology; Grondzik and Kwok, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings
questions.n: Required airflow is the air-change rate times the room volume.

questions.q: What is the main function of a damper in an air duct?
o: Filter dust out of the air stream
Reduce fan noise in the duct
Spread supply air across the room
Regulate or shut off airflow
questions.ref: ASHRAE 62.1 terminology; Grondzik and Kwok, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings
questions.n: Dampers are movable blades that balance, isolate or shut off airflow. Filters, attenuators and diffusers do the other jobs.

questions.q: A room must keep contaminants from escaping into nearby spaces, such as an isolation room or a toilet. At what pressure is it held?
o: Negative pressure relative to adjacent spaces
Positive pressure relative to adjacent spaces
The same pressure as the corridor
The same pressure as the outdoors
questions.ref: ASHRAE 62.1 terminology; Grondzik and Kwok, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings
questions.n: More air is exhausted than supplied, so air flows into the room under the door and not out of it.

questions.q: What is exhaust air?
o: Air returned from a room to the air handler
Air removed from a space and discharged outdoors
Air brought in from outside for ventilation
Air passed from one room to another
questions.ref: ASHRAE 62.1 terminology; Grondzik and Kwok, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings
questions.n: Exhaust air leaves the building for good. It is taken from toilets, kitchens and other places whose air should not be recirculated.

questions.q: What sets ventilation apart from air conditioning?
o: Ventilation controls humidity; air conditioning only moves air
They are the same process under two different names
Ventilation exchanges air; air conditioning also treats it
Ventilation always needs a fan; air conditioning never does
questions.ref: ASHRAE 62.1 terminology; Grondzik and Kwok, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings
questions.n: Ventilation dilutes and removes contaminants. Air conditioning treats the air: it cools or heats, dehumidifies, filters and distributes it.

questions.q: Why are outdoor-air intakes kept away from exhaust outlets and other pollution sources?
o: So intake noise stays away from the exhaust fan
So the ducts can be made shorter and cheaper
So rain cannot enter the exhaust outlet
So contaminated exhaust is not drawn back into the building
questions.ref: ASHRAE 62.1 terminology; Grondzik and Kwok, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings
questions.n: If an intake is too close to an exhaust, a plumbing vent or a loading dock, polluted air gets sucked back inside. Codes set minimum separation distances.

questions.q: Air passes through a 0.50 m² opening at an average of 2 m/s. What is the airflow?
o: 1.0 m³/s
4.0 m³/s
2.5 m³/s
questions.ref: ASHRAE 62.1 terminology; Grondzik and Kwok, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings
questions.n: Volume flow is the opening area times the average air speed through it.

questions.q: What is a louver at an outside-air or exhaust opening for?
o: Spreading supply air evenly across a room
Letting air through while keeping out rain and debris
Stopping fire from passing through a rated wall
Reducing duct noise with lined baffles
questions.ref: ASHRAE 62.1 terminology; Grondzik and Kwok, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings
questions.n: A louver has angled blades that shed rain and a screen that stops birds and debris, while air passes through.

questions.q: At what pressure is a clean room held to keep contaminants from getting in?
o: Negative pressure
The same pressure as the corridor
Positive pressure
The same pressure as the outdoors
questions.ref: ASHRAE 62.1 terminology; Grondzik and Kwok, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings
questions.n: More air is supplied than exhausted, so air leaks out through gaps and dirty air cannot leak in. Operating rooms work the same way.

questions.q: Which layout gives the best cross ventilation?
o: Openings only on one wall of the room
Large inlets and outlets side by side on the same wall
A sealed façade with a single small roof vent
Inlets and outlets on opposite sides of the space, with a clear path between them
questions.ref: ASHRAE 62.1 terminology; Grondzik and Kwok, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings
questions.n: Wind makes high pressure on the windward side and low pressure on the leeward side. Openings on both sides let air flow straight through.

questions.q: A room has only an exhaust fan. How does replacement air get in?
o: It leaks in through openings, drawn by the slightly lower indoor pressure
The exhaust fan pushes fresh air in through the same grille
Indoor pressure rises and forces outdoor air in
The return duct reverses and becomes a supply duct
questions.ref: ASHRAE 62.1 terminology; Grondzik and Kwok, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings
questions.n: Removing air lowers the indoor pressure a little, and outdoor air flows in through door undercuts, transfer grilles or gaps to replace it.
